https://www.dw.com/en/1-in-5-youths-targ.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5K1Xh A new survey by UNICEF found that one in five teenagers had been the target of online sexual abuse over the past year Image: Robin Utrecht/ROBIN UTRECHT/picture alliance Advertisement The internet is not a safe place for unsupervised children and young people — by now, that's common knowledge. Social media platforms are adept at tweaking their algorithms to ensure users of any age remain on their sites. To do that, they often disseminate content that can be dangerous and upsetting for young people. Studies regularly find a connection between what's known as doomscrolling and a higher risk of psychological problems in the young, including suicidal thoughts. And some of the latest trends in video creation on platforms like TikTok directly endanger the safety of users. In the United States, Meta, which owns both Instagram and Facebook, recently opted to settle a case against it out of court. A number of US states had claimed that the two platforms harmed children. In the court case against Meta, held in Oakland, California, the corporation avoided a conviction by reaching a financial settlement with states Image: Vicki Behringer/REUTERS Meta agreed to pay up to $17.1 billion (€14.7 billion) to the states involved and to limit teenagers' access to its platforms to just two hours a day. During the night, access will be completely blocked. A new survey by UNICEF , the UN agency for children, puts the spotlight on another danger that young people constantly face in the digital world: sexual assault , a threat experienced by one in five people between the ages of 12 and 17 over the past year. What are the key findings? The UNICEF report, which DW saw in advance of publication, explains how such attacks often happen. "It often begins without warning," the authors of the study wrote. "Conversation becomes coercion, and coercion becomes entrapment." The survey found that more than 15 million children had been exposed to unwanted sexual content. An estimated 9 million were pressured into sexual conversations or asked to share sexual images, while some 4 million had sexual images shared without their consent. The report's authors, however, warn that the true scale is likely far higher. "The report reveals a painful reality," said UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell. "These experiences cause profound emotional and mental distress. Many children suffer in silence, unsure where to turn for help." Often, the perpetrator of the assault puts pressure on a victim. The victims then feel ashamed and this makes it difficult to tell anybody about what has happened. Of those surveyed, 41% had never told anybody about their assault. Others said they had first confided in friends, siblings or their mothers. F ewer than 1% were reported to authorities. The stereotype many have of a complete stranger harassing young people online actually only applies in 16% of cases. Most perpetrators — 57% — are already known to their victims. They may be friends, family members or even romantic partners. In addition, 27% of respondents were not able to identify the people behind the profiles. When perpetrators are known, they include adults but also minors. In many cases, attacks take place in real life as well as online. The major social media platforms are also the main gateways for this kind of behavior. The UNICEF report says 60% of assaults come primarily from Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram (all of which are owned by Meta), followed by Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube . And 14% of respondents cited online gaming platforms as the location of an assault — gaming platforms usually have direct messaging channels. How was the data collected? The report polled around 21,000 young people in 21 countries, aged between 12 and 17, who regularly use the internet. Data from 12 countries — Ethiopia, Indonesia, Cambodia, Kenya, Malaysia, Mozambique, Namibia, the Philippines, Tanzania, Thailand, Uganda and Vietnam — had already been collected in 2020 and 2021 and analyzed in an earlier report. For this new report, additional data was collected in Armenia, Brazil, Colombia, the Dominican Republic, Mexico, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Pakistan and Serbia. The surveys were also supplemented by longer interviews with 100 young people who had experienced abuse. Children and young people can come into contact with potentially inappropriate AI-generated content online Image: Leon Neal/Getty Images Europe, US surveys find similar results Researchers familiar with this issue would not be surprised by the scale of the problem. The 2020 EU Kids Online Survey, based on a poll conducted in 19 European countries, indicated that 22% of all participants had received sexually explicit messages online. In a Spanish study conducted in seven secondary schools in 2021 and 2022, 21% of female respondents said they were sexually harassed online "occasionally," while 5% said this happened "frequently." For male respondents in the Spanish study, the percentages were a few points lower. A similar survey conducted by the Pew Research Center in 2022 found that 17% of 13- to 17-year-olds in the US said they had been sent explicit images without their consent. The survey did not differentiate between sexually explicit content and other material that showed things like violence. Social media bans in Australia, UK, France The UNICEF report calls on governments, tech companies and other stakeholders to better protect children and young people in the digital world. Among the requests: Design more secure digital platforms, with stronger protection for the privacy of minors. Strengthen national regulations and criminal law, and close loopholes. Establish trustworthy reporting and support systems for young people. Coming just after Meta's out-of-court settlement in the US, the new UNICEF report will likely add fuel to the fire for those seeking to ban social media for young people, an ongoing debate in many countries. In December 2025, Australia became the first country in the world to introduce an age limit for social media in order to protect minors. There, anyone under 16 is prohibited from having an account on platforms like YouTube, X, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat, a rule the platforms themselves are required to monitor. A similar age limit will come into effect in the UK in 2027, while France is the first EU country to have passed a law adopting an age limit — 15 years old — for social media users. However, it has since been blocked by France's top court, the Constitutional Council, which ruled it might infringe on freedom of expression and privacy. In June, a German commission proposed a tiered model. This would come with age limits, requirements for proof of age and strict rules requiring the cooperation of social media platforms. This article was originally written in German. https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text: Andy Burnham arrives at Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey on Wednesday evening. He will announce the new role there on Thursday morning. Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/Reuters View image in fullscreen Andy Burnham arrives at Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey on Wednesday evening. He will announce the new role there on Thursday morning. Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/Reuters Andy Burnham UK appoints world’s first special representative for climate security Exclusive: Madeleine Alessandri, chair of the joint intelligence committee, will take on the role of advising No 10 on climate-related national security risks Fiona Harvey in Antalya and Damien Gayle in London Wed 11 Nov 2026 17.30 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The UK government has appointed the world’s first special representative for climate security, in the strongest sign yet of fears that climate breakdown will bring chaos to the country. Prime minister Andy Burnham will announce the move on Thursday at Cop31, the UN climate summit, with the new role designed to advise the government on national security risks from the climate crisis before they spell catastrophe. Burnham will tell the key climate talks on Thursday morning: “We should all recognise the summer was not normal. The climate crisis is upon all of us now. We saw that with the wildfires that devastated lives and livelihoods everywhere.” This year’s summer was the UK’s hottest on record , with back-to-back heatwaves supercharged by the climate crisis causing health services and transport to suffer, schools to close and thousands of people to lose their lives prematurely. Burnham will add: “The message I carry here, in my first Cop as prime minister, is that the UK remains determined to reach net zero by 2050 and to work with our partners to build a clean energy future. The world has changed. The consensus we once enjoyed on science and climate action has broken down. “We will not stand by, and that’s why I’ve pledged a new era of British leadership over the next decade.” View image in fullscreen UK climate group Mothers Rise Up protest near Downing Street in September to highlight the impact of record-breaking heat on children. Photograph: Adrian Dennis/AFP/Getty Images Burnham arrived in Antalya, Turkey late on Wednesday night, before joining scores of heads of state and government for a series of high-level meetings at the talks, which are presided over jointly by Turkey and Australia. He will also confirm UK support for a proposed target of 35% electrification by 2035 and help towards plans to raise £5bn in private finance for clean energy projects across the world. Madeleine Alessandri, chair of the UK’s joint intelligence committee (JIC), which oversees MI5 and MI6, will take on the special representative job. But campaigners pointed to what they said were Burnham’s failures to take the measures needed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions at home, and to provide the funding needed to protect vulnerable countries overseas from the kind of risks the JIC has warned about. The government is mulling a major weakening of targets for electric vehicles and has given the green light to a gasfield , Jackdaw, in the North Sea while considering a new oilfield, Rosebank, west of Shetland. View image in fullscreen Climate campaigners protest outside the Department of Energy and Net Zero against the decision drilling at Jackdaw and Rosebank. Photograph: Denise Baker/Getty Images “What we’re seeing in part is double standards,” Mohamed Adow, director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank, told the Guardian. “We can’t have Britain preaching a clean development gospel but expanding fossil fuels back at home. You cannot expect one set of rules for Africa and another for Britain.” The UK’s credibility was “crumbling”, said Asad Rehman, chief executive of Friends of the Earth England, Wales and Northern Ireland. “The prime minister’s first climate talks should be an opportunity to demonstrate he means business. But if this is all the UK has to offer, then the questions piling in about his climate credibility are more than justified.” Under Alessandri, the JIC collaborated on a secret report warning that within five years the UK could begin experiencing national security impacts from the collapse of ecosystems overseas, driven by the climate crisis and overexploitation of the living world. These impacts included food shortages, rising food prices, mass migration and conflict among nuclear-armed countries. The report was suppressed under former prime minister Keir Starmer, but its contents were revealed by the Guardian last year , ahead of a redacted publication earlier this year. Dame Madeleine Alessandri said: “Climate change and nature loss are increasingly shaping the security environment in which the UK operates, placing additional pressure on resources, economies and communities around the world. “The best time to address these risks is before they develop into crises. In this role, I will work with partners across government and internationally to strengthen our understanding of climate threats, build resilience and ensure we are better prepared for the challenges ahead.” View image in fullscreen Low water levels in Colliford Lake reservoir, Bodmin Moor, Cornwall. This year’s summer was the UK’s hottest on record. Photograph: Amazing Aerial/Alamy The risks of the climate crisis to national security were also highlighted by Ed Miliband, foreign secretary, who has been briefing foreign capitals on the findings of the JIC report. He is also at Cop31 this week, and told the Guardian : “National security is the next frontier of the fight for climate action – the scenarios once of science fiction are now regular occurrences in the daily news.” He added: “Climate breakdown is one of the greatest national security threats we face: food security, threats to infrastructure and population movements [are resulting from the climate crisis]. “Those who seek to stick their heads in the sand on climate are putting our national security at risk.” In common with many wealthy nations, the UK has significantly rolled back its climate finance , funnelling money instead to military spending . In July, Burnham fronted a pledge to lower the cap on UK bus fares, funded by changing international climate donations into repayable loans. Prakash Dahal of Pro Public and Friends of the Earth Nepal said finance was vital for his country’s adaptation to climate breakdown, and recovery from disasters such as the catastrophic flash flood that struck Nepal in August. “Crucially, this essential funding must come as grants – not loans,” he said. “Nepal is not asking for charity. Nepal is demanding justice.” Explore more on these topics Andy Burnham Cop31 Climate crisis Global climate talks UK security and counter-terrorism Climate aid news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.dw.com/en/libya-suspected-dr.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PjRB Prefer DW on Google A satellite image shows huge plumes of smoke rising from a fire following an explosion aboard a Russian ship docked at the port of Benghazi Image: Planet Labs PBC/Handout/REUTERS Advertisement An explosion occurred early Sunday on a Russian ship at a naval base in Benghazi in eastern Libya due to a suspected drone attack. "Initial investigations indicate that the explosion occurred on board a Russian ship docked in the port," the eastern-based Libyan administration said in a statement. "It is suspected that the ship was attacked by drones." According to medical sources, injuries were reported, but no deaths. The statement added that, as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based Libyan government, the vessel had stopped at the Benghazi port to refuel and resupply on its way back to Russia. According to satellite imagery provider Vantor, the ship was the Merkury, a Russian Navy corvette. Imagery taken on Sunday revealed that the majority of the vessel had capsized and sunk, leaving only the bow visible above the water. Since the 2011 uprising that overthrew longtime dictator Moammar Gadhafi, Libya has been divided between the UN-supported government in Tripoli and a rival administration in the east backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar. Local authorities condemn attack The eastern-based administration said the port and naval base facilities in Benghazi, including the warehouses, were safe. They added that normal operations would resume once the fire was under control and the site was secured. The authorities condemned the suspected attack as a violation of Libya's sovereignty and a threat to maritime safety. They said they would take legal and diplomatic measures against those responsible and would launch a joint investigation with Russia. As of Sunday afternoon, no one has claimed responsibility for the suspected attack. The administration also stressed that Libya was not a party to the war between Russia and Ukraine or to any armed conflict beyond its borders. It said that its relations with friendly countries were a sovereign matter. It said it would not allow "Libyan ​ports, territory or territorial waters to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international ​conflicts." Second vessel hit near Benghazi Meanwhile, later on Sunday, two Libyan military sources told Reuters that a commercial vessel had been targeted by a drone boat off the coast of Benghazi. They added that Libyan naval forces had rescued the crew Libyan naval and air forces intercepted more than 12 naval drones, or drone boats, off the coast of Benghazi during the Sunday evening, according to Reuters sources. Echoes of Russia's war in Ukraine The incident in Benghazi occurred as Ukrainian forces increased their long-range attacks against Russia, extending far beyond the front lines. On Saturday, a drone hit a Russian cargo ship in the eastern Baltic Sea near Finnish waters. Finland's border guard said Ukraine carried out the attack. In March, a Russian tanker was attacked in the Mediterranean near Maltese waters. Libyan officials at the time believed this to be a sea drone attack. https://www.portfolio.hu/global/20261123.text: A kezdeti szakaszban a fő hangsúly az aknamentesítésen és a fel nem robbant lőszerek szakszerű hatástalanításán lenne, ám a sikeres végrehajtás később egy szélesebb körű katonai együttműködés alapjául is szolgálhat. A kiképzés a tavaly Jordániában felállított Damaszkuszi Koordinációs Központra (DCC) épülne. A tárgyalások alapján a misszióban mintegy tizenöt szövetséges ország – köztük Nagy-Britannia, Franciaország, Németország, Ausztrália, Szaúd-Arábia és az Egyesült Arab Emírségek – katonái is részt vennének. A katonai nyitás szorosan illeszkedik a Washington és Damaszkusz közötti fokozatos közeledés folyamatába, amely Basszár el-Aszad elnök 2024. decemberi megbuktatása után indult el. Az amerikai kormányzat 2025 decemberében feloldotta a Szíriát sújtó átfogó gazdasági szankciókat, 2026 augusztusában levette az országot a terrorizmust támogató államok listájáról, idén októberben pedig enyhített a fegyverexportra és a védelmi szolgáltatásokra vonatkozó korlátozásokon, lehetővé téve az engedélyek egyedi elbírálását. A közvetlen katonai segítségnyújtás előtt azonban mindkét oldalon komoly akadályok tornyosulnak. Az úgynevezett Leahy-törvények értelmében az Egyesült Államok nem támogathat olyan külföldi biztonsági egységeket, amelyeknél hitelt érdemlően felmerül a súlyos emberi jogi jogsértések gyanúja. Ezért az amerikai tisztviselőknek szigorúan át kell világítaniuk a programban részt vevő szíriai katonákat, különös tekintettel arra, hogy az új biztonsági erők több parancsnoka korábban iszlamista fegyveres csoportok tagja volt, és az ENSZ vizsgálói is dokumentáltak az új hatóságokhoz köthető visszaéléseket. Emellett a szíriai védelmi minisztérium egyes tisztviselői is vonakodnak attól, hogy beengedjék az amerikai katonákat a létesítményeikbe. A 2011 és 2024 között zajló polgárháború alatt az amerikai csapatok sem az Aszad-rezsimmel, sem a hatalmat végül átvevő szunnita lázadókkal nem működtek együtt, hanem főként a kurd erőket támogatták az Iszlám Állam elleni Inherent Resolve (Elszántság) hadművelet keretében. Az utolsó amerikai egységek idén áprilisban vonultak ki Szíriából, szeptemberben pedig Irakból. Murhaf Abu Kaszra szíriai védelmi miniszter és a hadművelet parancsnoka, Liam Hulin ellentengernagy Damaszkuszban egyeztetett a többnemzetiségű koordinációs mechanizmusról, a tűzszerész-kiképzésről, valamint a határvédelem lehetséges támogatásáról. Az egyik vizsgált forgatókönyv szerint a szíriai katonák kiképzése Jordániában és Szíriában párhuzamosan, korlátozott amerikai részvétellel már márciusban megkezdődhetne, a munkába pedig a Szíriai Nemzeti Aknamentesítési Központot is bevonnák. Az amerikai tisztviselők jelenleg azt vizsgálják, hogy a program finanszírozható-e az Inherent Resolve hadművelet fennmaradó keretéből, amely a becslések szerint megközelítőleg 200 millió dollárt tesz ki.
